Waterwell · section harvest

Best sections from the four concepts

The four 20 July concepts are recovered. This is what is actually worth lifting out of them and into the production site, and what is not. Pick the ones you want and I will port them one at a time, into the locked navy / cream + Instrument Serif system — not a rebuild.

Why the conditions section matters most right now. The site went from six conditions to ten today (six skin, four whole-body). The existing card grid was designed for six. Ten cards is the weakest thing on the page, so that section is the one worth fixing first — and both A1 and B1 solve it.

Candidates

Ranked. My recommendation on each, and why.

A1

Numbered conditions list

TAKE — highest valueDeep Current

Production uses a card grid. That was fine at six conditions; you now have ten, and ten cards is visual soup. A numbered list handles ten elegantly, reads as editorial rather than templated, and lets each condition carry a one-line 'what we actually do' note that the cards can't fit. It also groups cleanly — 01–06 skin, 07–10 whole-body — which keeps skin as the headline offer without hiding the rest.

Where it lands: Replaces the .cond-grid card grid in #conditions

B1

Dotted-leader contents index

ALTERNATIVE to A1The Dossier

Same job as A1, quieter execution. Reads like a journal contents page. Lighter on the eye and cheaper to build, but less confident and gives you nowhere to put the per-condition descriptions. Pick this over A1 only if you want the conditions section to recede rather than lead.

Where it lands: Alternative treatment for #conditions

C1

Alternating zig-zag process path

TAKERoot & Bloom

Production's four steps sit in a flat row of cards, which reads as a list of features rather than a journey. Alternating left/right with numbered nodes makes the progression physical — you follow it down the page. It's the single clearest upgrade to how the process is communicated, and it costs nothing in brand terms.

Where it lands: Replaces the .stones row in #how

A2

Process steps with meta labels

TAKE — merge into C1Deep Current

The detail worth stealing is the small meta label above each step: '15 MIN · FREE', '75 MIN'. It answers the two questions people actually have — how long, and does it cost — before they have to ask. Production buries both in body copy. Fold these labels into the zig-zag path rather than taking this layout wholesale.

Where it lands: Meta labels only, merged into C1

B2

Editorial belief with drop cap

CONSIDERThe Dossier

Production's belief section is a plain centred paragraph. This gives it weight — drop cap, two-column setting, and a pull-quote in Kohei's voice. It's the section that does the persuading, so it's worth more than plain text. Caveat: it's the most 'magazine' of the picks and pushes the site further editorial than it currently sits.

Where it lands: Restyles the belief block

A3

Four-up online reassurance row

CONSIDERDeep Current

A tight four-column answer to 'is online as good as in person' — from home / anywhere in the world / no traffic / same depth of care. Now that Kohei is Australia-based and everything is remote, this objection matters more than it did. Production handles it more loosely.

Where it lands: Tightens the online-care section

B3

Hero figure-stat callout

CONSIDERThe Dossier

A single hard number pinned beside the hero — 'FIG.01 / 75min — length of the initial consultation'. Concrete, verifiable, and it signals thoroughness without making a claim you'd have to substantiate. Cheap to add to the existing hero.

Where it lands: Adds a stat block to the hero

A4

Split story — quote / bio

SKIPDeep Current

Handsome, but production's story section already uses Kohei's real photographs, which beat a typographic treatment for trust on a practitioner site. Don't trade a real face for a nice layout.

Where it lands: —

D1

Hard-bordered specimen grid

SKIPVitals

Strong as a concept, wrong for this brand. The lab/monospace register reads clinical-cold, and the audience here is people with distressed skin who have already been through the medical system. Warmth is the differentiator, so this works against the positioning.

Where it lands: —
